body.heading: The switch is more expensive than it looks
paragraphs: Jumping between messages, tabs and tasks feels efficient because something is always moving. But each switch costs a little re-loading time: where was I, what was I about to do, what did that email actually say? Those small costs add up across a day.
Single-tasking is the alternative: one thing, given your full attention, until a chosen stopping point. It can feel strangely quiet at first, especially if your days are usually noisy.

body.heading: How to actually do it
paragraphs: Pick one task and give it a container: twenty-five minutes, one page, this pile of emails. Write the task on a sticky note where you can see it, so when your mind offers you five other things, the note answers for you.
Keep a “later” list beside you. When an unrelated thought pops up — and it will — jot it down in two seconds and return. The list holds the thought safely so your mind can let it go.

body.heading: Start with easy wins
paragraphs: Practise single-tasking where it is pleasant: one song listened to properly, one cup of tea drunk without a screen, one walk without a podcast. These small reps teach your attention that staying is allowed to feel good.
Then borrow the skill for work, one container at a time. You do not need a monk’s discipline. You need a sticky note, a later list, and a little patience with the quiet.

takeaway: One thing, one container of time, and a list to catch everything else.
